title: Bowing Backwards Down the Hall of Mirrors
subtitle: The Siamese embassy of Kosa Pan to Louis XIV and the French embassies to King Narai, 1685–1688
intro: On 1 September 1686 three Siamese ambassadors walked the length of the Grande Galerie at Versailles toward a silver throne, carrying a letter from King Narai of Ayutthaya, bowing so low and so often that the court talked of nothing else, and then backed all the way out so as never to turn from Louis XIV. The man at their head, Kosa Pan (Ok-phra Wisut Sunthon), was a foster brother of the king who sent him. For six months France looked at him, and he, with his scribes, looked at France.

The embassy was one half of a two-way traffic. In 1685 Louis XIV had sent the Chevalier de Chaumont to Siam, partly to win trade and partly in the hope, encouraged by missionaries and by Narai's Greek favourite Constantine Phaulkon, that the king might become Catholic. The French aims were plain: converts, commercial privileges, and, as it turned out, garrisons at Bangkok and Mergui. Kosa Pan sailed home with those garrisons in 1687, and in 1688 a palace revolution led by Phetracha killed Phaulkon, saw Narai die and drove the French out.

The record is lopsided, and this chapter says so. Kosa Pan's own report to his king is lost except for a fortnight at Brest, found by accident in a Paris mission archive in the 1980s; his letters of thanks from the Cape survive in French colonial files. Almost everything else about the Siamese in France was written by their hosts: the courtier Dangeau's terse diary, the Mercure galant's flattering serial, a master of ceremonies' later memoir. On the Siamese side the royal archives perished in 1767, and the chronicles that survive were compiled later.

The reciprocal gaze is richer. Choisy's daily letters and Chaumont's and Tachard's relations describe Narai's court in 1685; La Loubère, in 1687, studied Siam like an ethnographer and recorded what Siamese who had been to France said about French women, pictures and prices. Ok-khun Chamnan, a Siamese envoy wrecked on the South African coast in 1686, reached Europe in 1688; his story survives only as a Jesuit retold it. A French officer's prison diary from Mergui, printed in London, closes the story from inside the revolution.

Laid side by side, these eyes show two courts performing for each other: France measuring the envoys by their admiration, the envoys measuring France in feet and counting its trees, and each side's records about the other shaped by what it wanted. Where a date or detail rests on secondary summary rather than the text, it is marked approximate.
calendar_note: France had used the Gregorian calendar since 1582, and all French dates here are Gregorian (New Style). England still used the Julian calendar in 1688–90, ten days behind; the English translation of the Mergui officer's diary appears to keep the French officer's own Gregorian dates, but this is not certain. Siam used a lunisolar calendar: days were counted as waxing or waning days of a numbered lunar month, and the year was reckoned in the Chula Sakarat era (CS), which begins in 638 CE, with the new year falling around April (CS year ≈ CE year − 638 from April; so the embassy sailed late in CS 1047 by most reckonings, and the revolution of mid-1688 fell in CS 1050). Siamese documents also used the Buddhist Era: Coedès read the date of Kosa Pan's Cape letters as the second waning day of the eighth month of BE 2231, equated with 24 June 1687 — one year higher than the modern BE = CE + 543 rule, reflecting older Siamese reckoning and the April new year. The surviving fragment of Kosa Pan's diary is given in its English edition with Western dates. The French sources disagree on the audience date: Dangeau's diary gives 1 September 1686, while some modern summaries give 3 September; this chapter follows Dangeau.

eyes.name: Kosa Pan (Ok-phra Wisut Sunthon)
eyes.role: First ambassador of King Narai to Louis XIV, aged about 53; a noble of Mon descent whose mother had nursed the future king; later Phra Khlang (minister of trade and foreign affairs)
eyes.where: At sea on L'Oiseau, then Brest, the Loire road, Paris and Versailles; Flanders; back to Ayutthaya
eyes.vantage_label: the envoy being looked at, writing back to his king
eyes.form: notebook (embassy diary fragment) and dated letters
eyes.authenticity: Only a fragment survives: a contemporary Siamese manuscript copy, brought from Ayutthaya by a missionary, found in the 1980s in the archives of the Missions Étrangères de Paris (IRFA, volume 1081) when the bound volume fell and was found to contain Siamese script. It covers about 20 June to 4 July 1686, at Brest, and breaks off before the journey to Paris. Published in English as The Diary of Kosa Pan (Silkworm Books, 2002; trans. Visudh Busyakul, ed. Dirk Van der Cruysse and Michael Smithies). No firsthand Siamese record of the audience, the Paris months or the tour has been found. Two letters of 24 June 1687, under his seal, survive in the French colonial archives (published by George Coedès). The 'notebook' entries shown in the 2017–18 Versailles exhibition are an acknowledged modern fiction, not his words.
eyes.bio: Kosa Pan led the second Siamese embassy to France and is the only Siamese traveller of the 1680s whose own account of France survives, even in part. His scribes measured rooms, counted trees and puzzled over names for French foods, writing a report meant for King Narai. Back home he was drawn into the 1688 revolution, served the new king Phetracha as foreign minister, and was disgraced and died in 1699.

sources.title: IRFA (Missions Étrangères de Paris archives): the Kosa Pan manuscript
The Diary of Kosa Pan (2002), review in JRAS
G. Coedès, 'Siamese documents of the seventeenth century', JSS 14

eyes.name: François-Timoléon, abbé de Choisy
eyes.role: Abbé, man of letters and courtier, aged 41; coadjutor (designated substitute) to the French ambassador, attached in case Narai converted
eyes.side: France, embassy of the Chevalier de Chaumont
eyes.where: Aboard L'Oiseau; Ayutthaya and Lopburi (Louvo), autumn 1685; return voyage with Kosa Pan
eyes.vantage_label: French eyewitness in Siam, then shipmate of the Siamese envoys
eyes.authenticity: Written as daily letters to his friend the abbé de Dangeau (brother of the Marquis), published in Paris in 1687 as Journal ou suite du voyage de Siam; modern edition by Dirk Van der Cruysse (Fayard, 1995); English translation by Michael Smithies (Journal of a Voyage to Siam 1685–1686). No pre-1929 English translation is known, so no quotation is given.
eyes.bio: Choisy, notorious in his youth for living as a woman, joined the embassy as a pious convert and was ordained priest in Siam. His journal is light, gossipy and sharp-eyed, and it is the main day-by-day record of the voyage that carried Kosa Pan to France.

sources.title: Journal of a Voyage to Siam 1685–1686 (trans. M. Smithies), library record
Choisy at the Cape, 1685 (DBNL, R. Raven-Hart, Cape Good Hope)

eyes.name: Alexandre, Chevalier de Chaumont
eyes.role: First French ambassador to Siam, aged 45; a naval officer and Catholic convert charged with seeking Narai's conversion
eyes.vantage_label: French envoy at the Siamese throne
eyes.authenticity: Relation de l'ambassade de Mr le chevalier de Chaumont à la cour du roy de Siam (Paris, 1686); an English version appeared in London in 1687 (not checked here, so not quoted).
eyes.bio: Chaumont's mission was frankly religious as well as diplomatic: he pressed Narai to become Catholic and won only privileges for missionaries. His relation is the official mirror image of the later Siamese visit to Versailles: the French envoy fretting over how high to lift a royal letter.

eyes.name: Guy Tachard SJ
eyes.role: Jesuit mathematician, aged 34 in 1685; one of six 'king's mathematicians' sent with Chaumont; then Phaulkon's confidential go-between with Versailles
eyes.side: France / Society of Jesus; agent of Phaulkon
eyes.where: Siam 1685; return voyage with Kosa Pan 1686; Siam 1687; Rome 1688
eyes.authenticity: Voyage de Siam des pères jésuites (Paris, 1686), English 1688 as A Relation of the Voyage to Siam; Second voyage du père Tachard (Paris, 1689), which also records Ok-khun Chamnan's shipwreck narrative. Polished for publication and promotional of the Jesuit mission and of Phaulkon.
eyes.bio: Tachard sailed out with Chaumont, back with Kosa Pan, out again with La Loubère, and back once more as Narai's envoy to Louis XIV and the Pope. More than anyone he carried the secret plan for French troops in Bangkok, and his books sold the Siam mission to French readers.

eyes.name: Philippe de Courcillon, marquis de Dangeau
eyes.role: Courtier, aged 48, member of the Académie française; kept a daily court journal from 1684
eyes.side: France, the court of Louis XIV
eyes.authenticity: Dangeau's daily journal survives in manuscript and was published in full in 19 volumes (Soulié, Dussieux et al., 1854–60). Entries are terse and factual; English versions used here are modern, so digests only.
eyes.bio: Dangeau recorded the court as a ledger of who was received, where and how. His entries on the Siamese register protocol, the curiosity of the king, and the ambassadors' complaints about how provincial towns had treated them.

sources.title: Journal de Dangeau, Versailles research centre corpus

eyes.name: Jean Donneau de Visé
eyes.role: Editor of the Mercure galant, the court-approved monthly, aged 48
eyes.where: Paris and Versailles, following the embassy
eyes.authenticity: Voyage des ambassadeurs de Siam en France, four parts issued with the Mercure galant, Paris, G. de Luyne, 1686–87 (Sept 1686, Nov 1686, an undated third part, Jan 1687). Written to glorify Louis XIV; it reports the envoys' words second-hand and in French paraphrase. No pre-1929 English translation found.
eyes.bio: Donneau de Visé turned the embassy into a serial for French readers: every town's welcome, every speech, every visit to the Invalides or the Observatory. His pages are the fullest host-side record and the source of most of the envoys' remembered sayings.

sources.title: Voyage des ambassadeurs de Siam en France (1686–87), catalogue record

eyes.name: Nicolas de Sainctot
eyes.role: Maître des cérémonies at the French court, 1655–1691
eyes.vantage_label: the man who staged the reception
eyes.authenticity: Mémoires, compiled after 1709 from notes kept in office; BnF ms. français 14118 (copy presented to Louis XIV), transcribed by the Centre de recherche du château de Versailles (2015).
eyes.bio: Sainctot's job was to calibrate honour. His note on the Siamese reception shows the precise ranking behind the splendour: the embassy was to be received with full show but a notch below ambassadors of the great crowned heads of Europe.

eyes.name: Claude de Forbin
eyes.role: French naval officer, aged 29, left behind in Siam as admiral of Narai's forces and governor of Bangkok
eyes.authenticity: Mémoires du comte de Forbin (Amsterdam, 1730), ghost-written from his recollections by Reboulet decades later; vivid but self-serving and hostile to Phaulkon. Dates from it are approximate.
eyes.bio: Forbin saw the Siam that the Versailles audiences did not: Phaulkon's power, a bloody revolt by Makassar exiles, and a court he thought had no intention of converting. He left in disgust at the end of 1686.

eyes.name: Ok-khun Chamnan Chaichong
eyes.role: Siamese envoy, junior member of the embassy to Portugal; later interpreter and envoy to Louis XIV and the Pope
eyes.where: Shipwrecked near Cape Agulhas 1686; Bangkok 1687; Paris and Rome 1688–89
eyes.vantage_label: the other Siamese traveller, told through a Jesuit
eyes.authenticity: His story survives only as Tachard retold it in the Second voyage (1689); modern edition A Siamese Embassy Lost in Africa, 1686 (ed. M. Smithies, Silkworm, 1999). Not his own text; details passed through translation and Jesuit framing.
eyes.bio: While Kosa Pan was landing at Brest, Ok-khun Chamnan was starving on the South African coast after the Portuguese ship carrying a Siamese embassy to Lisbon broke up. He survived, came home, met the La Loubère embassy, then sailed to France and Rome himself.

sources.title: A Siamese Embassy Lost in Africa, 1686 (Silkworm)

eyes.name: Simon de La Loubère
eyes.role: Diplomat and mathematician, aged 45; envoy extraordinary of Louis XIV to Siam 1687–88
eyes.vantage_label: the reciprocal gaze: a Frenchman studying Siam
eyes.authenticity: Du Royaume de Siam (Paris, 1691); English as A New Historical Relation of the Kingdom of Siam (London, 1693) — pre-1929 English, so short quotations from it are given. Written after his return from notes made in Siam; more an ethnography than a diary.
eyes.bio: La Loubère spent barely three months in Siam but wrote the most systematic European account of it, from the alphabet to betel to court etiquette. He also recorded what Siamese who had been in France said about French women, pictures and prices.

sources.title: A New Historical Relation of the Kingdom of Siam (1693), full text

eyes.name: Claude Céberet du Boullay
eyes.role: Director of the French East India Company, aged 40; co-envoy with La Loubère for trade
eyes.where: Ayutthaya and Lopburi, then overland to Mergui, Dec 1687
eyes.authenticity: His journal of the 1687 embassy is published in English in Mission Made Impossible: The Second French Embassy to Siam, 1687 (ed. M. Smithies, Silkworm, 2002); details here rely on secondary summaries and are marked approximate.
eyes.bio: Céberet's business was the commercial treaty that confirmed Chaumont's 1685 terms. He crossed the peninsula to Mergui on the Bay of Bengal, a route that showed how much the French plan depended on garrisons at the edges of Narai's kingdom.

eyes.name: Anonymous French officer of the Mergui garrison
eyes.role: Junior officer under Du Bruant, commanding fifty Siamese soldiers at a small fort at Mergui
eyes.where: Mergui, then prisoner at Lopburi, Ayutthaya and Bangkok, June–Nov 1688
eyes.authenticity: Printed in English as an appendix to A Full and True Relation of the Great and Wonderful Revolution… in the Kingdom of Siam (London, for Randal Taylor; year on title page damaged, c.1689–90), based on letters from Siam of October 1688 and February 1689. The officer is unnamed; the French original has not been traced here.
eyes.bio: This short prison diary is the only day-dated eyewitness record in the chapter from inside the 1688 revolution. It shows the French garrison plan collapsing from the bottom: a man seized by the very soldiers he commanded.

sources.title: A Full and True Relation of the… Revolution in the Kingdom of Siam (EarlyPrint text)

eyes.name: Royal Chronicles of Ayutthaya (Phongsawadan Krung Si Ayutthaya)
eyes.role: Court chronicle tradition of the Siamese kings
eyes.vantage_label: the Siamese court's own memory, written later
eyes.authenticity: The Ayutthaya archives were destroyed in 1767; the surviving chronicle recensions covering 1688 were compiled or revised later (late 18th–19th century). They record Narai's death and Phetracha's accession but say almost nothing about the French embassies. English: The Royal Chronicles of Ayutthaya (trans. Richard D. Cushman, 2000).
eyes.bio: The chronicles give the Siamese state's view of 1688: a succession, not a foreign crisis. Their near-silence about the French is itself a measure of how differently the two courts weighed these years.

eyes.name: Engelbert Kaempfer
eyes.role: German physician in Dutch East India Company service, en route to Japan
eyes.vantage_label: a later visitor to the post-revolution court
eyes.authenticity: His account of Siam forms part of The History of Japan (London, 1727, trans. J. G. Scheuchzer from his manuscripts). Only the fact of his meeting with Kosa Pan as minister is used here.
eyes.bio: Kaempfer passed through Ayutthaya two years after the revolution and met the former ambassador, now running foreign affairs for King Phetracha: a coda seen by an outsider with no stake in the French project.

entries.headline: Sailing for Siam with a king's letter and six Jesuits
entries.digest: Choisy left Brest on the warship L'Oiseau, with the frigate La Maligne, in Chaumont's embassy. Aboard were the two Siamese envoys of 1684 going home and six Jesuit 'king's mathematicians'. He had promised the abbé de Dangeau a letter every day, and the journal grew from that promise.
entries.source_note: Choisy, Journal (1687); date in DBNL Cape notes and critiqueslibres review of the 1995 edition.

entries.place: Table Bay, Cape of Good Hope
entries.headline: Anchoring under the Dutch fort at the Cape
entries.digest: After a hard passage the ships anchored off the Dutch Cape colony. Salutes were traded with the fort and the Dutch commissioner-general, Van Reede, was ashore; the Jesuits set up to observe for longitude. The stop lasted a week, until 7 June.
entries.source_note: DBNL (Raven-Hart, Cape Good Hope 1652–1702), Choisy's Cape entries of 30 May–7 June 1685.

entries.place: Bar of the Chao Phraya, Siam
entries.headline: Landfall at the mouth of the Menam
entries.digest: The embassy reached the bar of the river below Bangkok after almost seven months at sea. Choisy's journal turns from shipboard boredom to the first sight of Siamese officials sent down to greet the ambassador. Sources place the arrival on 23 or 24 September.
entries.source_note: Arrival 23 Sept (ayutthaya-history chronology) or 24 Sept (Orchiston et al., JAHH 2016).

entries.headline: Handing Louis XIV's letter up to a king at a window
entries.digest: Chaumont was received in solemn audience by King Narai, who sat at a raised window above the hall. The French envoy, carrying Louis XIV's letter in a gold cup, would not lift it to the window's height, and the king leaned down to take it. Chaumont used the audience to urge Narai toward Catholicism.
entries.source_note: Date: Orchiston et al. (JAHH 2016) and ayutthaya-history chronology. The letter-height episode is from Chaumont's and Choisy's relations as commonly summarised; not checked against the 1686 text.

entries.headline: Watching the audience from the ambassador's suite
entries.digest: Choisy, standing behind Chaumont, described the hall, the prostrate mandarins and the king's window. He was quicker than Chaumont to see that Narai welcomed the French for trade, Jesuit learning and a counterweight to the Dutch, not for baptism.
entries.source_note: Choisy, Journal, entries for October 1685 (Smithies trans.); content summarised, not checked line by line.

entries.headline: Ordained a priest in Siam
entries.digest: In the last weeks of the mission Choisy received holy orders from the French missionary bishop in Siam, the culmination of the conversion that had brought him on the voyage. He treated it in the journal as both solemn and faintly comic, a courtier made priest at the far end of the world.
entries.source_note: Ordination in Siam: ayutthaya-history.com Choisy page and catalogue notes; exact day not verified.

entries.headline: Left behind as Narai's admiral and governor of Bangkok
entries.digest: Forbin was named admiral and general of the King of Siam's forces and governor of Bangkok, a post Phaulkon arranged and Forbin had not sought. In his later memoir he presented it as a trap: he was to stay while the embassy sailed home. The same day Chaumont and Phaulkon signed an agreement granting privileges to French missionaries.
entries.source_note: Ayutthaya-history chronology (10 Dec 1685); missionary agreement in Orchiston et al., JAHH 2016. Memoir framing from Mémoires (1730).

entries.headline: A lunar eclipse observed beside King Narai
entries.digest: Tachard and the other Jesuits set up their telescopes for a total eclipse of the moon, and King Narai came to watch, looking through their instruments. For the Jesuits this was the high point of the mission: European astronomy displayed to an Asian king who was interested in it, if not in conversion.
entries.source_note: Orchiston et al., 'Jesuit astronomy in Siam', JAHH 19 (2016): eclipse visible on the morning of 11 Dec 1685; Tachard, Voyage de Siam (1686).

entries.headline: Farewell audience at Louvo
entries.digest: Chaumont took formal leave of Narai at Lopburi. He left with a commercial agreement and missionary privileges but without the conversion he had come for, and with a Siamese embassy to carry back to France.
entries.source_note: Ayutthaya-history chronology gives 12 Dec 1685 for the farewell audience.

entries.headline: Kosa Pan sails for France
entries.digest: Kosa Pan and the second and third ambassadors, Ok-luang Kanlaya Ratchamaitri and Ok-khun Si Wisan Wacha, embarked with their suite, letters and gifts. Tachard sailed with them carrying Phaulkon's secret proposals. No Siamese text survives from the voyage itself.
entries.source_note: Departure 22 Dec 1685: ayutthaya-history chronology; DBNL Tachard Cape notes. Members: Wikipedia, Kosa Pan.

entries.place: Table Bay, Cape of Good Hope
entries.headline: Homeward at the Cape among the Dutch Indies fleet
entries.digest: On the return voyage L'Oiseau anchored at the Cape among seven Dutch ships of the Indies fleet, after calling at Bantam in January. The Siamese envoys were aboard; Tachard's interest was in observations and in Dutch eyes on the French.
entries.source_note: DBNL (Raven-Hart), Tachard's Cape entries for 10–13 March 1686.

entries.headline: A Siamese embassy wrecked on the African shore
entries.digest: The Portuguese ship carrying a Siamese embassy to Lisbon broke up off the southern tip of Africa. Ok-khun Chamnan reached shore with other survivors, wet and almost naked, on a coast without water or food. Over about a month they walked toward the Dutch colony, eating what they could find and leaving the weakest behind.
entries.source_note: Date: Wikipedia, Ok-khun Chamnan; narrative from Tachard, Second voyage (1689), per Japan Times review of Smithies ed. (1999).

entries.headline: Cherries, artichokes and a green-curtained bed
entries.digest: At a Brest feast the envoys tasted five kinds of fruit; the cherry, written phonetically in Siamese, became a favourite. The scribes were unsure of names for foods such as the artichoke and recorded their guesses. They described the ambassador's canopied bed, its curtains all in a green they likened to banana leaves.
entries.source_note: Japan Times review (29 June 2003) of The Diary of Kosa Pan (2002); individual entry dates not checked.

entries.headline: Home with three Siamese ambassadors
entries.digest: L'Oiseau and La Maligne returned to Brest, closing the circle that had opened there fifteen months before. Choisy's journal ends with the landing; the Siamese embassy he had sailed with began its long stay.
entries.source_note: Return 18 June 1686: critiqueslibres review; Versailles 'key dates' page; ayutthaya-history chronology.

entries.headline: The surviving Siamese record begins
entries.digest: Two days after landing, the embassy's scribes began the entries that survive. They wrote for King Narai and set down what could be measured: rooms in feet, trees in the gardens, the guns of the port. Paper had run out, so they wrote on odds and ends.
entries.source_note: IRFA: the diary runs from 20 June to 4 July 1686; Japan Times review (2003) on contents and the paper shortage.

entries.headline: The diary breaks off before Paris
entries.digest: The surviving manuscript stops at Brest, just before the embassy set out by road and river for Paris. Everything Kosa Pan later reported about Versailles, the court and the tour is lost, and is known only through French eyes.
entries.source_note: IRFA (diary ends 4 July 1686); Japan Times review (breaks off before the march to Paris).

entries.headline: Part one of the Mercure's Siamese serial
entries.digest: Donneau de Visé issued the first part of Voyage des ambassadeurs de Siam en France: the receptions in each town on the road from Brest, the entry into Paris and the audience. The envoys are shown as grave, observant and full of questions. He stressed Kosa Pan's great interest in French maps and pictures.
entries.source_note: Voyage des ambassadeurs de Siam en France, vol. 1 (Sept 1686), catalogue description; map interest cited in Wikipedia, Siamese embassy to France (1686).

entries.headline: Fighting the Makassar rebels
entries.digest: While the envoys were being shown off in France, Forbin at Bangkok was caught up in Phaulkon's measures against Makassar exiles in Siam, whose revolt of 1686 was put down with heavy loss of life. His memoir tells it as a story of his own courage and Phaulkon's ruthlessness; it is the opposite of the courtly picture of Siam being painted at Versailles.
entries.source_note: Ayutthaya-history chronology (orders to Forbin against a Makassarese ship, 27 Aug 1686); Mémoires de Forbin (1730), written later. Casualty figures in sources vary and are not given here.

entries.headline: A throne at the end of the gallery
entries.digest: Dangeau recorded that the king received the Siamese on a raised throne at the end of the gallery by the Dauphine's apartments, with the abbé de Lionne interpreting. The three ambassadors came to the last step to hand up their king's letter, bowed very low, and withdrew backwards so as never to show the king their backs. He noted the suite of four gentlemen and two secretaries, and that the second ambassador had served in China and was meant to compare France with it.
entries.source_note: Dangeau, Journal, 1 Sept 1686 (English version, partylike1660); Versailles key-dates page.

entries.headline: Grading the honours: a marshal, but not a prince
entries.digest: Sainctot, writing years later from his notes, explained the ceremonial choice. The king sent the Maréchal de La Feuillade to fetch the envoys, using his title as colonel of the guards to make it look grander, because he meant to receive them a degree below ambassadors of crowned heads, who were escorted by foreign princes.
entries.source_note: Mémoires de Sainctot, t. II (BnF ms. fr. 14118), 'Réception faite aux ambassadeurs de Siam en 1686'; written after 1709.

entries.headline: Fifteen hundred spectators and a letter in a box
entries.digest: The Mercure described the envoys passing along a route lined with the king's silver furniture, about 1,500 people watching, and the king, ill with a fistula, holding the audience regardless. The Siamese were allowed to look at the king, against their own custom, and withdrew backwards with hands joined. Leaving the medal cabinet afterwards, one of the party was reported as saying he now knew a fourth greatness after Man, God and Paradise: Versailles.
entries.source_note: Château de Versailles key-dates page (summarising contemporary reports, chiefly the Mercure galant). The 'fourth greatness' saying is a reported remark in French, not from a Siamese text.

entries.headline: Giving the word of command to French infantry
entries.digest: The day after the audience the Siamese went to see the works at Maintenon. Infantry were drawn up under arms in their honour, officers saluted them with pikes, and the envoys were invited to give the word of command to the troops. Dangeau summed it up: every honour was paid them.
entries.source_note: Dangeau, Journal, 2 Sept 1686 (partylike1660).

entries.headline: Kind words at court, rough welcomes in the provinces
entries.digest: Dangeau noted that the king often saw the Siamese in his small apartment, treated them with great courtesy and let them walk the gardens freely. They were delighted with him, but complained of poor receptions in several towns on their journey, Orléans above all. They meant to see the king's conquests in Flanders but not Alsace, because the cold already troubled them, and they kept asking if the winter would be long.
entries.source_note: Dangeau, Journal, 2 Oct 1686 (partylike1660).

entries.headline: Gifts for the Dauphine, and Phaulkon's escape plan
entries.digest: The king judged the ambassadors' presents to the Dauphine very handsome and was pleased with gifts from 'Monsieur Constance', Narai's Greek favourite Phaulkon. Dangeau added that Phaulkon asked for Louis's protection and seemed to be thinking of retiring to France if his master died.
entries.source_note: Dangeau, Journal, 5 Oct 1686 (partylike1660).

entries.headline: Invalides, Observatory, Saint-Cyr: a programme of wonders
entries.digest: The second part of the Mercure's serial covered the envoys' audiences with the Dauphine, the princesses of the blood and the ministers Croissy and Seignelay, and their visits to Versailles, Saint-Germain, Marly, Clagny, the Invalides, the Observatory and Saint-Cyr. The tour was arranged to show French power, learning and piety, and the reports measure the visitors by their admiration.
entries.source_note: Voyage des ambassadeurs de Siam en France, vol. 2 (Nov 1686), catalogue description.

entries.headline: Flanders, a fête at Saint-Cloud, and farewell
entries.digest: The fourth part followed the envoys home from Flanders by way of Valenciennes, through the harangues of town corporations, a festival given by Monsieur at Saint-Cloud, and their farewell audience. It listed the gifts they received and the people going out to Siam with them, and noted seventeen audiences crammed into a single day.
entries.source_note: Voyage des ambassadeurs de Siam en France, vol. 4 (Jan 1687), catalogue description.

entries.headline: Leave-taking from Louis XIV
entries.digest: Kosa Pan and his colleagues took formal leave of the king after weeks of negotiation over trade and the French request for posts in Siam. Louis XIV's reply to Narai praised the ambassador's conduct and credibility. The envoys' own report of the farewell does not survive.
entries.source_note: Date 14 Jan 1687: Château de Versailles 'Kosa Pan' long-read; Louis XIV's letter quoted in Wikipedia, Kosa Pan. Not confirmed in Dangeau here.

entries.headline: Sailing with the envoys and the soldiers
entries.digest: La Loubère and Céberet sailed from Brest with the returning Siamese ambassadors, Tachard and his Jesuits, and General Desfarges' troops destined for Bangkok and Mergui. The soldiers were the real cargo: the treaty Kosa Pan carried home would be tested by garrisons.
entries.quote: we set Sail from Brest on the First of March, Anno 1687
entries.source_note: La Loubère, A New Historical Relation (1693), opening; Céberet (Wikipedia).

entries.headline: Thank-you letters from the Cape, under his seal
entries.digest: From the Cape the three ambassadors wrote to the Marquis de Seignelay, thanking him for the favours shown them in France, praising Louis XIV and pledging lasting friendship; they expected to reach Siam within three months. A second letter to the East India Company director Lagny asked him to send the presents left behind and to prepare the Siamese boys left in France to come home.
entries.source_note: Coedès, JSS 14 (1921), letters in French colonial archives dated in the Siamese calendar, equated with 24 June 1687.

entries.headline: Home, with stories no one quite believed
entries.digest: Kosa Pan returned to Siam with the French squadron and resumed his place at Narai's court. French writers later said the returning envoys found their accounts of France met with disbelief at home; no Siamese text of his report has been found.
entries.source_note: Return with La Loubère fleet: Wikipedia, Kosa Pan. Disbelief motif is a French report, not checked here.

entries.headline: Anchoring off the bar
entries.digest: The squadron anchored off the mouth of the river below Bangkok, seven months out of Brest. The French troops went up to the fortress at Bangkok, while the ambassadors waited for the Siamese ceremonies of reception to be arranged.
entries.quote: cast Anchor in the Road of Siam the 27th of September
entries.source_note: La Loubère, A New Historical Relation (1693). Ayutthaya-history gives 26 Sept and 6 Oct for different ships.

entries.headline: Receiving the French embassy
entries.digest: Home via Batavia after his African ordeal, Ok-khun Chamnan was in Bangkok to receive La Loubère and Céberet. He would soon be chosen to go to France and Rome himself.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Ok-khun Chamnan; Wikipedia, Simon de La Loubère (embassy received by Ok-khun Chamnan, Oct 1687).

entries.headline: What the Siamese said about French women
entries.digest: La Loubère recorded that two Siamese who had been in France said they were not at first struck by French women, but soon decided they alone were handsome. Shown pictures of French ladies, other Siamese joked that France must have better betel than theirs. Two young mandarins priced a life-size French doll at a hundred catis and said no one in Siam could afford her.
entries.quote: they presently apprehended that they alone were handsom
entries.source_note: A New Historical Relation (1693), part II; the conversations are undated within his stay.

entries.headline: Crowds bow to a letter, not to a Frenchman
entries.digest: La Loubère described the river procession of seventy or eighty state barges carrying the king of France's letter, and Siamese coming down from their houses to prostrate themselves as it passed. He judged that they did it out of reverence for the royal letter rather than curiosity. The solemn audience followed.
entries.quote: less out of curiosity for the Show, than out of respect
entries.source_note: Audience date: Céberet (Wikipedia), ayutthaya-history. Description: A New Historical Relation (1693).

entries.headline: A commercial treaty in three languages
entries.digest: Céberet concluded the commercial treaty at Lopburi, essentially confirming Chaumont's 1685 terms. Copies were drawn up in Siamese, French and Portuguese; the Siamese text is dated by the lunar calendar. Louis XIV ratified it only in February 1689, after Narai was dead.
entries.source_note: Coedès, JSS 14 (treaty of 11 Dec 1687, copies in French colonial archives); Céberet (Wikipedia).

entries.headline: Meeting Forbin on the road to the Bay of Bengal
entries.digest: Travelling overland to Mergui, Céberet met Forbin at Tenasserim. Forbin, by now out of Siamese service, gave him a dark view of Phaulkon and of French prospects in Siam.
entries.source_note: Ayutthaya-history chronology (30 Dec 1687); content of the conversation summarised from Forbin's later memoir and secondary accounts.

entries.headline: Leaving on bad terms with Phaulkon
entries.digest: La Loubère sailed from Siam on the Gaillard, having quarrelled with Phaulkon. With him went Tachard, now Narai's envoy, and a new Siamese mission under Ok-khun Chamnan bound for Versailles and Rome.
entries.source_note: La Loubère, A New Historical Relation (1693): 'the 3d of January, 1688'; Wikipedia, La Loubère.

entries.headline: Second voyage west, this time to the Pope
entries.digest: Ok-khun Chamnan sailed with Tachard and two other mandarins as envoys to Louis XIV and Pope Innocent XI. In France and Rome he would tell Tachard the story of his shipwreck, which Tachard published the next year.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Ok-khun Chamnan.

entries.headline: Escorting Desfarges back to the French fort
entries.digest: The day after Phaulkon's execution, Kosa Pan was one of two mandarins who went with General Desfarges to Bangkok to receive the fortress for Phetracha. Once inside, Desfarges's officers decided to resist, and the siege began. The former ambassador to Versailles now stood on the other side of the French garrison.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Siege of Bangkok (6 June 1688; Phaulkon executed 5 June).

entries.headline: Seized by his own soldiers
entries.digest: Commanding fifty Siamese soldiers at a small fort at Mergui, the officer was seized by his own men and chained to a stake for four days. On 29 June he was taken out to identify French dead after Du Bruant's retreat and questioned under torture about Du Bruant's plans.
entries.quote: I was seized on by my own Men, and made Prisoner
entries.source_note: A Full and True Relation… (London, c.1689–90), appended officer's diary, 25 and 29 June.

entries.headline: The death of King Narai
entries.digest: The chronicle tradition records Narai's death at Lopburi and the passing of power to Phetracha, without the French framing of plot and poison. European sources give 10 or 11 July.
entries.source_note: Death 11 July: Orchiston et al. (JAHH 2016), Wikipedia Siege of Bangkok; 10 July in some sources (ayutthaya-history). Chronicle wording not checked.

entries.headline: A bishop brings peace terms
entries.digest: Brought as a prisoner to Lopburi and questioned by the chief minister, the officer heard from a missionary that the French bishop had gone to Bangkok to negotiate. On the 25th the bishop returned with full powers from Desfarges, and the treatment of the French prisoners eased.
entries.quote: the Bishop return'd to Louvo with full power
entries.source_note: A Full and True Relation…, officer's diary, 17–25 July 1688.

entries.headline: Phetracha crowned
entries.digest: Phetracha was crowned king at Ayutthaya, founding a new dynasty. The officer's diary notes that the French and English held at Siam and Lopburi were released the day after the coronation.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Siege of Bangkok (coronation 1 Aug 1688); officer's diary in A Full and True Relation. Chronicle text itself not checked.

entries.headline: Peace signed at Bangkok
entries.digest: After about two months held near Bangkok, the officer recorded the signing of the peace that let Desfarges's garrison leave Siam. On 2 October he was sent back to Mergui to find Du Bruant and tell him.
entries.quote: On the 30th of September the Peace was concluded and signed
entries.source_note: A Full and True Relation…, officer's diary, 30 Sept and 2 Oct 1688; Wikipedia, Siege of Bangkok (agreement late Sept).

entries.headline: A French ship at last
entries.digest: Back at Mergui after searching the rivers for traces of Du Bruant, the officer found the French ship Cocq and embarked about two days later for Pondicherry. The next day, 13 November, Desfarges's garrison sailed from Bangkok.
entries.source_note: A Full and True Relation…, officer's diary, 12 Nov 1688; French departure from Bangkok 13 Nov: Wikipedia, Siege of Bangkok.

entries.headline: Before Pope Innocent XI
entries.digest: Ok-khun Chamnan and the other Siamese mandarins had their first audience with Pope Innocent XI, unaware that the king who sent them had died in July. Their farewell audience followed on 5 January 1689; in February the trade treaty was ratified at Versailles.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Ok-khun Chamnan.

entries.headline: The ambassador of Versailles, now minister of a closed court
entries.digest: Passing through Siam on his way to Japan, Kaempfer met Kosa Pan, by then Phetracha's minister for foreign affairs and trade. The French were gone; the Dutch, whose company Kaempfer served, remained.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Kosa Pan (Kaempfer met him in 1690); month not verified.

entries.headline: Disgrace and death
entries.digest: Accused of sympathy for the French and loyalty to Narai's memory, Kosa Pan was mutilated on Phetracha's orders and disgraced. Dutch accounts say he took his own life. The court archives that might have held his full embassy report were destroyed with Ayutthaya in 1767.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Kosa Pan (death 15 Nov 1699, per Dutch accounts); Japan Times review (c.1700).

claims.claim: The French envoy treats the height of a royal letter as a question of national honour, and presses a Buddhist king to convert
claims.evidence: Chaumont, Relation (1686), as summarised in modern accounts

claims.claim: Narai shown as a curious patron of European astronomy, a sign the Jesuits read as openness to their faith
claims.evidence: Tachard, Voyage de Siam (1686); Orchiston et al. 2016

claims.claim: France recorded as things to measure and name: room sizes, tree counts, guns, cherries, artichokes, a green-curtained bed
claims.evidence: The Diary of Kosa Pan (IRFA ms. 1081; Silkworm 2002)

claims.claim: The envoys portrayed as devoted admirers of Louis XIV, keenly interested in French maps and pictures
claims.evidence: Voyage des ambassadeurs de Siam en France, vol. 1

claims.claim: Siam ranked one notch below Europe's crowned heads: honoured by a marshal, not a foreign prince
claims.evidence: Mémoires de Sainctot, t. II (written after 1709)

claims.claim: The Siamese backing away from the throne noted with approval; the second envoy said to have been sent to compare France with China
A Siamese visitor reported as calling Versailles a fourth greatness after Man, God and Paradise
claims.evidence: Contemporary French report, summarised by Château de Versailles

claims.claim: The envoys complain that provincial France, Orléans above all, received them badly, and dread the coming winter
Phaulkon seen at court as a client seeking French protection and a retirement in France
France's fortresses, festivals and corporations staged for Siamese eyes, down to seventeen audiences in one day
claims.evidence: Voyage des ambassadeurs de Siam en France, vol. 4

claims.claim: France thanked for its favours; friendship pledged; the Siamese boys left in France to be readied for home
claims.evidence: Letters to Seignelay and Lagny, French colonial archives (Coedès, JSS 14)

claims.claim: Siamese prostrations read as reverence for the royal letter, not for the French themselves
Siamese returned from France said French women alone were handsome; others joked about French betel and priced a French doll in catis
claims.evidence: A New Historical Relation (1693), part II

claims.claim: The Siamese soldiers under French command turn on their officer as the revolution reaches Mergui
claims.evidence: A Full and True Relation… (London, c.1689–90), appended diary

claims.claim: The fall of Narai and Phetracha's accession recorded as a Siamese succession, with the French barely visible

convergences.label: Chaumont's audience with King Narai at Ayutthaya
convergences.note: The ambassador's relation dwells on protocol and the conversion plea; Choisy, behind him, notices what Narai actually wanted. Fifteen months later the same choreography of letters and bows would be staged at Versailles with the roles reversed.

convergences.label: Last days at Lopburi: eclipse, appointments, farewell
convergences.note: On 10–12 December the Jesuits watched an eclipse with the king, Forbin was made governor of Bangkok against his will, missionary privileges were signed and Chaumont took leave. Each saw a different Siam: a patron of science, a trap, a mission field, a diplomatic success.

convergences.label: The embassy sails west with Kosa Pan aboard
convergences.note: French and Siamese envoys share one ship for six months; the French journals survive, the Siamese record of the voyage does not.

convergences.label: Landing at Brest, while another Siamese embassy is lost in Africa
convergences.note: As Choisy's journal closes and Kosa Pan's scribes begin counting trees at Brest, Ok-khun Chamnan's party, wrecked in April, has only lately staggered into the Dutch Cape colony after a month on foot: two Siamese embassies to Europe, one feted, one half-starved.

convergences.label: The audience at Versailles
convergences.note: Three French records of one ceremony: Dangeau notes the throne and the backward retreat, Sainctot the calibrated rank, the Mercure the crowd and the compliments. Kosa Pan's own record is lost. In the same weeks Forbin, in Bangkok, was fighting the Makassar revolt, a Siam no one at Versailles was describing.

convergences.label: The return voyage, with troops
convergences.note: The returning ambassadors share the fleet with the soldiers meant for Bangkok and Mergui. La Loubère's report and Kosa Pan's thank-you letters from the Cape speak of friendship; the cargo spoke of garrisons.

convergences.label: La Loubère's reception in Siam
convergences.note: Now the French are watched: Chamnan receives them, the returned envoys talk of France, and La Loubère studies Siamese manners as closely as the Mercure had studied Siamese bows.

convergences.label: Departures from Siam
convergences.note: A French embassy leaves on bad terms with Phaulkon, carrying a Siamese one that will reach Rome only after its king is dead.

convergences.label: The revolution and the siege of Bangkok
convergences.note: The former ambassador to Versailles escorts the French general to be dispossessed; at Mergui a French officer is chained by his own soldiers; the chronicle later records only a change of king.

ties.note: Choisy's journal was written as daily letters to the abbé de Dangeau, brother of the diarist Marquis de Dangeau.
Shipmates on L'Oiseau from December 1685 to June 1686.
Chaumont's embassy carried Kosa Pan's embassy back to France; Chaumont accompanied it at Versailles.
Tachard sailed with the envoys both ways and acted as Phaulkon's confidential agent alongside them.
Tachard took Chamnan to France and Rome in 1688 and published his shipwreck narrative in 1689.
Dangeau's journal records the ambassadors' audiences, visits and complaints.
The Mercure's four extraordinary parts are the fullest French record of Kosa Pan in France.
Both at court on 1 September 1686, one staging the ceremony, one recording it.
They met at Tenasserim on 30 December 1687 and sailed together from Mergui on 3 January 1688.
Chamnan received La Loubère's embassy in Bangkok in October 1687 and sailed home with him in January 1688.
Kosa Pan travelled back to Siam in La Loubère's fleet in 1687.
In 1688 Kosa Pan served Phetracha in dealing with the French garrisons; the officer was a prisoner of the same revolution.
Kaempfer met Kosa Pan as minister at Ayutthaya in 1690.

threads_out.note: The Ottoman envoy Yirmisekiz Mehmed Çelebi came to the French court in 1720–21 and was received by the same ceremonial machinery and reported in the same Mercure, a generation after Kosa Pan.
The two silver cannons presented by the Siamese embassy were kept at the Invalides and, according to the Château de Versailles, were seized by the crowd in July 1789 on the way to the Bastille.

Kosa Pan's diary survives in the archives of the Missions Étrangères de Paris, whose bishops were in Siam in the 1680s; it was an MEP priest, Bernard Petitjean, who met Japan's hidden Christians in 1865.

The Jesuit 'king's mathematicians' sent with Chaumont carried telescopes to Siam and observed the eclipse of 11 December 1685 with King Narai, extending the telescope's reach from Europe to an Asian court.

images.title: Louis XIV Receiving the Siamese Ambassadors (medal)
images.caption: Silver medal by Jean Mauger commemorating the audience of the Siamese embassy, struck to publicise the event; gold medals of this kind were among the king's gifts to the second and third ambassadors.
images.credit: Jean Mauger; The Metropolitan Museum of Art

images.title: Tribute of the Siamese ambassadors to the King
images.caption: Copper engraving after Pierre-Paul Sevin, engraved by Cornelis Vermeulen, in Tachard's Voyage de Siam (Paris, 1686): the French image of the embassy published while the envoys were still in France.

images.title: Hearing granted by the King of Siam to the French Ambassador
images.caption: Period engraving of Chaumont's audience with King Narai in 1685, the king at a raised window above the hall: the reciprocal scene to Versailles.

images.title: The Siamese Ambassadors before the King
images.caption: Image catalogued as 'The Siamese Ambassadors before the King', 1686, attributed to Charles Le Brun, who also drew Kosa Pan's portrait and guided him through the Hall of Mirrors.
images.credit: Attributed to Charles Le Brun; Heritage Images

images.title: Kosa Pan at Versailles (Château de Versailles)
images.caption: The château's page reproduces Le Brun's 1686 portrait of Kosa Pan (Louvre), the Almanach of 1687 engraving of the audience and the BnF medal. Its 'notebook' text is a modern reconstruction, not Kosa Pan's diary.
images.credit: RMN-Grand Palais; Château de Versailles; BnF
